title: Cyber Kill Chain
summary: The Cyber Kill Chain is a seven-stage model of an intrusion that describes how an adversary progresses from reconnaissance to mission impact. The stages are reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives. Its purpose is not to describe every intrusion precisely but to give defenders a shared vocabulary and a set of choke points where activity can be detected or disrupted before the adversary reaches the final stage. The model rests on an asymmetry: the adversary must succeed at every stage, while defenders need to break only one link, which reframes defence as cost imposition rather than perfect prevention. In practice the chain is most useful for structuring detection coverage reviews, sequencing incident narratives and choosing controls. Hardening the external attack surface targets reconnaissance. Mail and web filtering target delivery. Patch management and exploit mitigations target exploitation. Application control and endpoint hardening target installation. Network monitoring and egress control target command and control. Data loss prevention, backup integrity and segmentation limit actions on objectives. The model has well-known limitations. It was written with perimeter intrusion in mind, so it maps awkwardly to cloud identity attacks, supply-chain compromises, insider activity and hands-on-keyboard operations that skip or reorder stages. It is also linear, while real intrusions loop, repeat and run stages concurrently. Analysts therefore commonly pair it with ATT&CK for technique-level detail and with the Diamond Model for actor and infrastructure context. Used with those caveats, the kill chain remains a durable briefing tool because non-specialist stakeholders can follow it, and it exposes where an organisation has no detection at all rather than merely where its tools are noisy.
objectives: You will be able to name the seven Cyber Kill Chain stages and place observed activity into the correct stage.
You will be able to identify the choke points where a control or detection can break the chain before impact.
You will be able to explain why the model fits perimeter intrusions better than cloud identity or supply-chain attacks.
You will be able to translate a kill-chain coverage review into a prioritised list of missing controls.
You will be able to combine kill-chain narrative structure with technique mapping in a single incident write-up.
You will be able to brief non-specialist stakeholders using chain stages without overstating the model's precision.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: The Cyber Kill Chain is a seven step model of how an intrusion unfolds. It starts with planning and ends with the attacker reaching their goal. Each step is a chance for defenders to break the attack. The steps are reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives.
beginner.whyItMatters: The attacker must succeed at every step, but you only need to stop one. That is a huge advantage. The model helps you see where your defences have holes. Maybe you detect delivery well but never notice an attacker quietly controlling a machine. Naming the stages also gives your team and your managers a shared language. You can then fix the weakest link instead of buying more tools.
howItWorks: Reconnaissance. The attacker studies your company, your staff and your public systems before doing anything.
Weaponisation and delivery. They build a harmful file or link and send it by email or a fake website.
Exploitation. A bug in your software lets the attacker run their code on one of your machines.
Installation. The attacker plants something on the machine so they can return after a restart.
Command and control. The infected machine quietly calls home to receive its orders.
Actions on objectives. The attacker steals data, encrypts files or damages your systems.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar trying to enter your home. First they watch the house and note when you leave. Then they pick a lock or copy a key. Then they slip inside. Once in, they prop open a back door so they can return easily. Finally they carry out your television. You could stop this at any point. A light on a timer spoils the watching, a strong lock spoils the entry, and a loud alarm spoils the escape.
takeaways: The attacker must win at every stage, while you only need to break one link.
Use the seven stages to find where your detection coverage is missing.
The model fits older network attacks better than cloud, supply chain or insider threats.
